In a few days, on the first of July, we shall be celebrating Canada Day, as it is commonly referred to by our news media, commentators, politicians and by the Canadian public. However, the status of Canada Day has yet to be officially sanctioned by law. Consequently, whereas the Constitution was patriated on April 17, 1982, and it would be entirely appropriate to celebrate that event on Canada's birthday, I move, seconded by the hon. members for Bonaventure-lles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bujold), Roberval (Mrs. Beauchamp-Niquet) and Levis (Mr. Gourde):

Madam Speaker, I had intended to put my question today to the Minister of Finance but he is, right this minute, outside the House of Commons giving television interviews when he should be here answering questions.
I will put my question to the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister knows that Canada is suffering from a crisis in confidence. Inflation has increased 2.4 per cent since February, 1980; unemployment has increased by over 350,000 people; interest rates have increased by over 3 percentage points, and the Canadian dollar has fallen almost ten cents since this government came into office.
In view of the fact that economic conditions are the worst in over 40 years, does the Prime Minister realize that this is the most important budget that will have been presented in the House of Commons during his term of office and that it cannot simply be a cosmetic update of last year's November budget?

Madam Speaker, it goes without saying that the Minister of Finance is very much aware of the many problems facing our country and other western countries. He does not need the hon. member's rhetoric to make him aware of these problems, and he is equally aware that there is a limit to the resources available to the government to cope with them. With the means at his disposal, the minister will try to deal with these problems as satisfactorily as is possible and help Canadians get through the present difficult period.
If the Minister of Finance felt so strongly about these economic problems, why does he not have the guts to be here to answer these questions?

Madam Speaker,
I will ask my supplementary question of the Prime Minister. Due to the failure of the Minister of Finance to design a budget last year to address the economic problems today, and because that budget, in fact, compounded the economic problems of today, will the Minister of Finance, in the face of this failure, follow the accepted parliamentray tradition and offer his resignation to the Prime Minister before presenting this new budget so that the Prime Minister will have the flexibility to accept a new man to put a fresh face on economic policy in this country?

Madam Speaker, I do not quite understand the nature of the
hon. member's question. He is complaining about the fact the Minister of Finance is not in the House today-the minister is in the House as often as he can be-while the hon. member has previously been fond of complaining that the Minister of Finance does not give press interviews or does not make enough speeches outside the House, and now, when he does, the hon. member has the gall to complain. I would ask him to please be patient on both counts, and to wait until Monday, when he will realize that the Minister of Finance has a very clear grasp of the problems besetting Canadians and that he is more than competent to respond to the present situation.
Possibly the Prime Minister is indicating who his new Minister of Finance will be.

Madam Speaker, let me ask a question which must be answered by the Prime Minister. Yesterday the value of the Canadian dollar dropped following the announcement that there would be a budget speech. There is uncertainty in the market today. There will continue to be uncertainty until Monday night when the budget is brought down. Would the Prime Minister take this opportunity to allay that uncertainty in the marketplace by stating whether or not the government is proposing to continue the monetary policy it has been following and whether or not the stabilization of the Canadian dollar will be a primary objective of this forthcoming budget speech?

Madam Speaker, the hon. member is wondering about our fluctuating dollar and trying to see the dollar's fluctuation as a sign. He should have wondered-if his leader would stop talking, perhaps the member for Etobicoke Centre could at least have the courtesy, I would not say to listen but to at least make a pretence of listening to the answers. Respect for Parliament, Madam Speaker, starts here. So instead of starting to wonder during the past few days about the downward pressure on the dollar, the hon. member should look at what has been happening for several months and stop looking for simplistic causes for phenomena that are infinitely complex.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 am not in a position to answer the hon. member's question but I will take the matter up with the minister concerned.

The House resumed from Tuesday, June 22, 1982, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pepin that Bill C-92, an act to amend the National Harbours Board Act, the Government
Harbours and Piers Act, the Harbour Commissions Act, the Canada Shipping Act and the Fishing and Recreational Harbours Act, be read a second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport.

Madam Speaker, our purpose today is to resume debate of Bill C-92, which began on June 14, 1982, and continued on June 22. Before I do so, I would like, with your indulgence, to respond to a remark made in the House a few moments ago by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) with respect to the designation of the national holiday as Canada Day. He had occasion to refer specifically to me. I want him and other members on that side of the House to know that what is at stake in the celebration of this national holiday is not the name of the day, be it Canada Day, Dominion Day or Confederation Day, but the spirit Canadians demonstrate on that day, as well as the sense of oneness they have. That sense is not developed or helped by the President of the Privy Council when he makes those kinds of remarks in the House of Commons. Just let me add this warning to him; that if he is to show any maturity and judgment as the conductor of House business, he ought not to make such remarks that are designed and calculated to stir up resentement among people across Canada at a time when we should be bringing those people together in a common purpose.
Let me review some of the remarks I made on June 22 respecting Bill C-92. I said that members of the House ought to examine the new legislation with a critical eye but with an open mind. If the new provisions establish a sensible and sound national ports policy and an efficient and effective organization structure to implement that policy, then the cause of the Canadian maritime transport industry will be substantially advanced. However, the marine transport industry in Canada and internationally will have to bear the burden in the future of any legislative mistakes that are made now. Therefore, we must examine and assess Bill C-92 with great care.
In mentioning the Canadian marine transport industry, allow me for a moment to reflect upon the contributions made by my colleague from Nova Scotia, the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall). In 17 years of service in the Parliament of Canada, the hon. member has continued to advance the cause and interests of the marine transportation industry. That interest is evidenced in this bill and in predecessor bills in the formation of which he had a great hand. On behalf of the people in the port of Halifax, the Province of Nova Scotia and indeed those across Canada who are interested in marine transportation, I want to make it clear that we appreciate the contribution he has made to that industry in the bill which is before us now.
In my remarks on June 22 I reviewed the operation of the National Harbours Board as it functions today. I said that the board has already implemented an internal decentralization program with respect to its personnel and control of operations. The board has been more than aggressive, in some cases regressive, in its cost-recovery program. The result is a net income of $59.8 million in 1981, an increase of $42.5 million over 1980.
June 23, 1982

However, much of that increase relates to the generous debt forgiveness afforded the National Harbours Board by the Government of Canada, of approximately $500 million. Let us not give too much credit to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) and the National Harbours Board. We know that similar refinancings have bailed out the Canadian National Railways and the St. Lawrence Seaway in the past. Let me underline my comments that the eastern Canadian ports of Halifax, Saint John, Quebec City and Montreal are in severe competition and that the National Harbours Board is perceived to favour the Quebec ports because almost half of that $470 million in debt write-offs, or $231 million, relates to the port of Montreal. Only $30 million was allocated to the port of Halifax, which is only about 8 per cent of that total amount. Therefore, Your Honour can see why suspicions of favouritism in the administration of the National Harbours Board policy are rampant on the east coast. When one considers the allegations of sweetheart deals approved by the National Harbours Board to assist and advance the cause of the Cast group in the port of Montreal and the help given to the Canadian Pacific group to provide facilities in Montreal to lure Dart Container Lines from the port of Halifax, one quickly realizes why Nova Scotians watch this federal government agency with a wary eye. But now the question is, what are the hopes and expectations for the future? Will this new national ports legislation achieve those hopes and fulfil those expectations?
Let me now deal with the port of Halifax and how it may be affected by this legislation. I hasten to add that Halifax, along with Saint John, Quebec, Montreal and Vancouver, is regarded by Charles N. Forward as one of Canada's five great seaports. He described the port of Halifax in an excellent article in the "Urban History Review" as a "magnificent natural harbour." The harbour is immense in size, has a great depth of 50 feet very near the shore, is ice-free and has a very low tidal range of under three feet. The harbour and the adjacent Bedford basin easily accommodated immense convoys during World War II. Therefore, very clearly, the port of Halifax is both Canada's gateway and its guardian.
Let me consider the port of Halifax in the current economic context. I have already indicated that on the one hand, it is in fierce competition with the port of Saint John for cargo destined for the east coast of Canada and, on the other hand, it is in severe and fierce competition with the port of Montreal and the port of Quebec for all eastern Canadian cargo. What has happened as a result of this competition in these depressing economic times is that the port of Halifax suffered a downturn in 1980 and 1981 in the amount of cargo handled over the years. In 1981 it had a gross registered tonnage through the port of 21,417,000, which was a slight increase over the previous year. But, taking into consideration other, more effective aspects of the total cargo, it had a substantial decrease. For example, container traffic was down 8 per cent, to 1,785,000 tonnes.
The downturn in the economy has contributed to the slight increase in traffic compared to the port of Montreal, but what is more important are the difficulties which have been
Canada Ports Corporation Act
experienced in the port of Halifax because of the existing competition and the favouritism which has been shown toward the port of Montreal. Specifically, let me refer to the loss of Dart Container Lines. Dart Container Lines accounted for approximately one third of the container traffic through the port of Halifax and, in turn, accounted for a substantial amount of the total cargo through the port of Halifax. In 1981, it moved its operations to the port of Montreal as the result of an arrangement with the Canadian Pacific group. The loss of Dart was a tremendous blow and caused a disadvantage to the port of Halifax. It has left the container facilities in the port of Halifax substantially unused.
The Fairview Cove container terminal which came on stream during 1981 is experiencing some difficulties, but the fact that it is utilized by the Polish Ocean Lines leads to some hope for the future. There is also hope that other lines can be attracted to the port of Halifax at both the Halterm container terminal and the Fairview Cove container terminal and that this very important segment of cargo can be substantially increased in the years ahead.
Mr. Speaker, very much a part of the national ports legislation is the capacity and capability of a national port to achieve self-sufficiency. In the last full year, which was 1981, the port of Halifax managed to reduce its deficit by some $4 million, so that with respect to its operation during the year, it has accomplished self-sufficiency. It really deserves the status of a national port on the basis of self-sufficiency, that is to say, return of revenue from its operations. I will deal with the other aspects of the national ports determination later. But let me consider the application of the national ports policy contained in Bill C-92 in more general terms.
I want to deal with that national ports policy in the context of the national transportation policy as that policy is enacted by the National Transportation Act. The national ports policy is contained in Clause 2 of the bill, which would enact a new Section 3 of the act. Clause 2 states:
"3. (1) It is hereby declared that the objective of the national ports policy for Canada is to create a port system that
(a) is an effective instrument of support for the achievement of Canadian
international trade objectives and of national, regional and local economic and
social objectives;
Also as part of that national ports policy, it will be declared in the new section of the act that the ports be efficient, provide access and equal treatment for the movement of goods and, in addition, that local port corporations have a high degree of autonomy. If one reviews that enunciation of the national ports policy in the context of the total national transportation policy, one will find that the national transportation policy involves:
-an economic, efficient and adequate transportation system making the best use of all available modes of transportation at the lowest total cost ... to protect the interests of users of transportation-
I put those words on the record simply to demonstrate that there is an element of rhetoric in these statements of policy, whether in the national ports policy or in the national transportation policy. It is very difficult to look at the words as they are enshrined in statutory provisions and determine from those

June 23, 1982
Canada Ports Corporation Act
words what will take place in the future, both with respect to the operation of our national ports and with respect to the operation of our national transportation system. Therefore, when we refer to policy in terms of the statutory words used, we must recognize and realize that we are only referring to an academic matter. We are not discussing the reality or what the system will be when it is implemented. Therefore, it is a matter of placing faith in the agencies, in the branches and in the departments of government which administer these policies.
1 must say that Canadians have very little basis for placing much faith in the agencies and departments of the Government of Canada from their experiences with those agencies and departments over the past two or three years since this government took office. They have not provided any economic impetus or stimulus to Canadians or to Canadian industry, whether involving the transportation industry, the automobile industry or any other industry. I want to underline that point simply by saying, in conclusion, that while we may establish a statement with respect to a national ports policy, or while we may make a statement with respect to national transportaton policy, that statement is useless and meaningless unless it is given full and proper implementation by a concerned and knowledgeable government department or agency.
The other major thrust of Bill C-92, as I have indicated, is the new corporate structure which will be utilized in the administration of our national ports system. The major features of that structure, as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) pointed out in his address during the second reading of Bill C-92, involved a maxi-corporation to replace the current National Harbours Board and a series of mini-corporations which will operate the specific national ports to which the legislation will be applied.
I have already dealt with the National Harbours Board. I want to point out and underline to members of the House and interested persons across Canada that there may be no substantial difference in the establishment of a new Canada Port Corporation if it simply carries on with the same attitudes, policies and philosophies of the National Harbours Board as it now exists.
There is an indication in the legislation that there may be substantial differences between the Canada Ports Corporation and the National Harbours Board. Specifically, the Canada Ports Corporation will have a board of directors. If that board simply functions as the membership of the National Harbours Board has in the past, there will be no real benefit.
This is not the first time the Government of Canada has come forward with legislation in the House which changes the status of an existing service or agency and promotes or changes it into another kind of corporation. We saw that in the Canada postal service which evolved into the Canada Post Corporation. I feel safe in saying that to date users of that service have not noticed any substantial difference in the service they are receiving. People have not noticed any substantial difference in the attitude of the persons involved in that service. Maybe those changes will come. We should give the Canada Post
Corporation time to effect those changes. However, it serves to underline the fact that merely changing the name or the corporate structure changes nothing unless you change the personnel involved and their attitude toward the performance of their service.
The Canada Ports Corporation will continue to be operated as a national agency. It will continue to be controlled by the Government of Canada. It will continue to be based in central Canada, and probably will continue to have many of the same personnel and players who were involved before. In that respect, the members may ask whether there will be any susbtantial change.
The Minister of Transport assured us of one thing. The chairman of the National Harbours Board, Pierre Franche, will not be staying in that post. With all due respect to him, that may be the most promising sign of this new legislation, that we will get a new look and a new face on this national organization. I do not have to tell Mr. Franche that he is not the most popular person in eastern Canada. He goes there from time to time and hears complaints, but only rarely does he make those visits.
A very good man.

Let me talk briefly about the mini-corporations. As I understand it, there are 15 ports which will qualify for this mini-corporation status as local port corporations. The requirements are that the ports have regional and national significance, that they demonstrate local interest in the port and that they have the capacity and capability to become selfsufficient. Those are sensible criteria for the establishment of a national port. I have no doubt that the ports in which I have a special interest, the port of Halifax and the port of Saint John in the neighbouring province of New Brunswick, will qualify quite easily.
What really is at the heart of this kind of legislative provision is the people who will operate the corporation. That is where I have great concern for this legislation. First, with respect to the port authorities that are now in place in our national ports, the port of Halifax and the port of Saint John, the minister has never undertaken to permit labour representation on the local port authority. Anybody who is familiar with the operation of a port knows what a vital role labour plays in the operation, and knows that without the co-operation of a capable labour force, the port simply will not function.
How the Minister of Transport, through or with the concurrence of the National Harbours Board, can construct a local port authority that does not have labour representation is beyond my belief. The minister must know that I have requested time and again that organized labour in the form of the International Longshoremen's Association or one of the other unions involved with the waterfront be represented on the port authority for the port of Halifax. My request has gone begging-
I have to say that if there is not going to be any change in
that attitude and if there is to be no recognition of the role that
June 23, 1982

labour plays and no change in policy with respect to appointments to the boards of local corporations, I do not anticipate or expect much to flow from this legislation. We have to face the fact that this legislation will simply provide another vehicle to which members and supporters of the Liberal Party can be appointed.
I hate to say it in the presence of the Minister of Transport, who has been so reasonable on other matters, but on our port authority for the port of Halifax we have not one, but two, defeated Liberal candidates. The minister has been broadminded. He appointed one person who was defeated in a provincial election and one person who was defeated in a national election. In that sense he has both local and national representation. He is not dealing solely with national Liberals or provincial Liberals. He has taken one of each and put them on the port authority.
I hope the minister does not intend to put them on the board of directors of any local corporation that may be established for the port of Halifax. If he does that, that local corporation, as the manager of the port of Halifax, will lose all credibility and this legislation, it if is ever passed, will come crashing to the ground.
With that warning, I say to the minister that basically the concept is good. If he can resist the demands of his supporters and friends in the Liberal Party of Canada, and, in the case of the port of Halifax, of Nova Scotia, and appoint persons who really have the qualifications, the bill can be successful. As 1 said, it could be a forward step in the marine transportation industry.
I have to say in specific terms that the qualifications listed in this statute for appointment to the board of a local port corporation are in such general terms that I am afraid there will be the same patronage that existed in the past. The directors of local port corporations appointed by governor in council only need to have the experience and capacity required for discharging their function and will be representative of the regional and local populations and interested in management of the port. As I said, if that simply means you have to get Liberal supporters with local interests and Liberals supporters with national interests, the purpose and effect of the legislation may well fail.
Let me deal with one more specific aspect of Bill C-92, the provisions that relate to revenue, both the use of revenue and such matters as borrowing for the ports. There is real concern that the Canada Ports Corporation will utilize those revenue provisions to get total control of the port system and use those revenue provisions to destroy the autonomy that is supposed to be given to national ports under the provisions of Bill C-92. Everybody knows that he or she who controls the purse strings controls the operation. If we simply go through the exercise of having elaborate statutory provisions and give the financial control completely to the central body, we will not have real autonomy. That is a matter we have to look at very carefully.
I want to speak very briefly about the public harbours aspect of Bill C-92. As we know, 500 public harbours across Canada are governed by the provisions of the Government Harbours
Canada Ports Corporation Act
and Piers Act. Those harbours will be brought within the framework of this Bill C-92 as part of the over-all national ports system.
Again, Mr. Speaker, if you will look at the technicalities of this, you will know that the small public harbours across Canada are really operated by the harbour master, and that the success of that operation depends upon the capacity and capability of that particular officer.
If he or she is knowledgeable and is able to contribute to the management of the harbour, then the harbour will be successful, providing effective and efficient service to the users. But again, if it is simply used as another tool for patronage for the Liberal Party-which it is, and I can document that with thousands of cases-then again the whole purpose of the exercise of this new legislative provision will be lost.
1 will not dwell on this point Mr. Speaker. I hate to face the Minister of Transport with these realities of life because I am sure he is not involved in them himself personally. In my province of Nova Scotia, unless you are a member of the Liberal Party, you do not get to be a wharfinger unless you have this political connection. I want to stop that and stop it right now, because it is too dangerous. The ports are too important to the local economy, too important to the fishermen and to others in transport and users who are involved in that port activity, to allow it to be governed in that fashion. I hope that the minister will change that aspect of this operation.
Now I would like to speak for a moment in very general terms about the importance of a national ports system. As a resident of the Province of Nova Scotia and as the Member of Parliament for Halifax West, I fully appreciate the importance of the marine transportation industry. It provides thousands of vital jobs in the Halifax metropolitan area and in other parts of Nova Scotia, like Sydney. In Sydney there is a port that is capable of expansion and extensive growth. There is the Strait of Canso which has tremendous possibilities as a marine transport terminal. We regard marine transportation as vital to the future of Nova Scotia, particularly with respect to offshore development.
We want the system to work. I can speak for myself and I am sure I can speak for my colleague for Dartmouth-Halifax East and my colleague for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan), who is also our transportation critic and who is very interested in ports policy. We want to co-operate to ensure that we do have an effective national ports policy, that we have an effective national ports system. We are all willing to work constructively to this end. At the same time, the Minister of Transport and those who deal with him in the Department of Transport and in other aspects and other departments of government interested in transport, all have to work to change their ways. They have to work to implement, once established, an effective national ports policy.
This is one of those many things where, if we all work together-those in Parliament and those who are called upon

June 23, 1982
Canada Ports Corporation Act
to administer the legislation that Parliament enacts-if all those elements work together, then we will achieve something for the benefit not only of the people of the port of Halifax, not only for the people of Nova Scotia, but for all Canadians.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-92, which deals with national harbours and ports. 1 want to begin by pointing out that there is only one member of the New Democratic Party in the House-and he is only partly in the House. It may give an indication of the level of interest of that party in this legislation. It is fortunate that it is their caucus representative who is on the Transport committee. I would like to begin by referring to the remarks that member made, the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), in the House, when he took issue with the speech made by my colleague for North Van-couver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook). The member for Regina West rose in his place to say:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. gentleman who just concluded his remarks: where was he in the last two years in the Transport committee.
Then he went on to say:
The guy has never shown up for a bloody meeting; he has never been there!
Those are not my remarks, those are the remarks of the erudite member for Regina West. It is not quite the kind of vocabularly I am used to using. Then he went on to say:
My point of order was a simple question. Is the hon. gentleman going to start appearing at Transport committee meetings?
I would like to ask the member for Regina West whether you have to be consistently a member of the Transport committee in order to speak on the transport bill in the House. Or do you have to be a member of the health and welfare committee in order to speak on a health and welfare bill in the House? Do we have to pass a credentials layout from the member for Regina West before we have permission to speak in the House? I recall very well that just prior to the speech by my colleague, the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby that his colleague for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) gave us a 40-minute speech in the House. I have just checked the record of the committee membership and I do not find her name on the list of members of the committee. Yet she gave us a 40-minute lecture most of which was a history of ports legislation and had very little to do with the content of the bill. Yet the member for Regina West has the audacity to lecture the rest of us on how and when we can speak in this House. I think that is offensive. It is certainly a little hard to speak to this particular bill because I do not think the minister who is in charge of this legislation has any long-term historical precise interest in this legislation. I do not say he has to design all of his interest to a specific area-except that if he is responsible for the legislation he had better give some attention to it. I think he would rather be reading the latest edition of the Pepin-Robarts report. That is fine.
I am here listening to you now.
Well, I know, but you are here listening to me because it is such a treat, not because you are so interested in the legislation.
Oh, oh!

It would be a help if the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) had all of his intuitive attention riveted on transport issues rather than on other issues. It is a little difficult to deal with this legislation knowing full well that it is not the minister who designed the legislation, nor is it going to be the minister who will make the final disposition of the particular provisions within the legislation. It will be the senior bureaucrats in his department who will make or break all of the sections of this particular bill.
I came here almost eight years ago, Mr. Speaker, short of about two weeks. I remember very well my first election campaign because I was very concerned about the major installation in my constituency known as the Fraser River Harbour Commission. Because of my concern about the relationship of that commission port to my municipality-
Now, the minister is leaving. Here is his last chance for an education, and he is walking out.
I will read it in Hansard.

Because of my continuing interest in the relationship of the commission port to the municipality of Surrey, I took interest in it during that campaign. I asked questions, on the convening of the House, as soon as I was elected, regarding the status of that commission port. It has been an eight-year interest of mine regarding this ports legislation. So I would simply point out to the member for Regina West that even though I have not been a member of the Transport committee I do have a major installation in my constituency which is of concern to me, and I think that is enough of a ticket to allow me to speak in this House. So with his permission I will go on and address myself to the concerns I have.
That is not enough.

That is not enough? Well, I will go ahead anyway, with your indulgence. Mr. Speaker, it bothers me that the legislation before us has gone through several mutations in the past eight or ten years. It began with the Scott report about eight years ago, for which we waited months and literally years. Then we had three of four bills tabled in the House before we could really get a full-fledged debate on this legislation. If a reorganization of the ports administration in Canada was so urgent, we should have done it a long time ago. Now that we have the legislation before us, it seems to me that the latest mutation this legislation has brought about is really not enough of an improvement over the past organization to make it desirable for the country.
I can understand the kind of DREE mentality that exists in
the government regarding some of the ports in Canada. There
June 23, 1982

are ports which deserve to function and operate as federal ports because they are a service to their areas. They may not necessarily be profitable in a cash flow situation or on a balance sheet, but they do form a very valuable function for the entire country. For example the port of Churchill can operate only about two months of the year, yet it is an important link in the transportation system in our country. So I understand the DREE mentality the government has about some of the ports of Canada.
However, why, under the design of this legislation, should the government treat all of the harbours in Canada which are presently National Harbours Board ports, the same way? Why should there be a kind of super board in Ottawa which directs or has its fingers in the operations of all of the National Harbours Board ports and then have about 15 local harbour commissions which report and are actually controlled by that super board in Ottawa? If it is necessary because of socioeconomic reasons for the federal government to be involved in the administration of some ports because the economics are not right for a profit-making structure, I will grant that, but why should the federal government be controlling and manipulating those ports which are profit-making ports? Why should the port of Vancouver be subject to the designs, manipulations and directives of the super board in Ottawa? Surely if that is a viable port-and the volume within that port would seem to indicate that it should be-and surely if the expertise in management is there in Vancouver-and I think it is, after all the experience-it should be able to divest itself of the paternalism of the federal government.
The minister has come back in. I have tickled his fancy. He will correct me later on.
The reason is that the port of Vancouver is of interest to other provinces, Alberta, Saskatchewan and so on. It is in Canada.
The minister says the reason is that the port of Vancouver is of interest to B.C., Alberta and Saskatchewan. Isn't that wonderful?
Yes.
To all of Canada.
That is what I said.

Is it not wonderful to think that those interests will be served only if Ottawa looks after them? Will the managers of the port of Vancouver not look after the interests of Alberta and Saskatchewan? Oh, those poor people in the western provinces! Will the managers of the port of Vancouver not look after the rest of Canada? Only Ottawa thinks of all of Canada; isn't that wonderful? It warms the cockles of my heart-
What heart, Benno?

-to think of the great way the super board in Ottawa will look after all of Canada, but those people in
Canada Ports Corporation Act
British Columbia who manage that port at Vancouver are not very loyal Canadians and will not look after the rest of Canada! I think those British Columbians have a right to feel insulted by that kind of an inference.
I say to the minister that paternalism may have its place, but only in those areas where ports are not in a position to be independent. Paternalism has its place, but where ports can be independent, why should Ottawa control them, manipulate them and, in effect, strangle them? Why, under the provisions of this legislation, should the Vancouver port have to have its budget and operations ratified by Ottawa? If it makes money, why should it divest itself of its profits by sending them to Ottawa, as the provisions of this bill indicate?
No, you are wrong.
That is a concern I have.
You are wrong.

This is a Vancouver problem, and I know my colleagues who represent the harbour area of Vancouver will look after it. Those colleagues are the hon. member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon), the hon. member for Capila-no (Mr. Huntington) and the hon. member for North Vancou-ver-Burnaby. They will look after that matter both here and in committee, but I want to address myself to the concerns I have about the Fraser River Harbour Commission. It happens to be a very well-run operation. It is very well managed. In 1972 it had a net income of $626,836; in 1973 it had a net income of $1,265,005; in 1974, $1,466,616. The profits grew until 1981, when the Fraser River Harbour Commission had a net income of $5,158,755. I take my hat off to the managers of that operation. They are making money, and they are making money because the port is a commission port. That is one of the big reasons. The minister shakes his head. He will not give credit to Chris Brown, his Liberal friend, who operates that port.
That is not what I said.
It happens that Chris Brown is the chairman of the board there. He is a defeated Liberal candidate.
He couldn't get into the Senate.

He happens to be a very sharp businessman and is making money. I would like to give credit to him and the port manager, Mr. Rick Pearson, for doing a good job in spite of the fact that Mr. Brown is a Liberal. He is a very lonely man. However, they are managing the port well. The port is showing a profit because they do not have to have all their actions approved by Ottawa. They can act independently. They can borrow money and invest it. They can buy without having to turn the profits back to Ottawa. These people can plan; that is healthy, and I think the model of the harbour commission ought to be the model for other ports in Canada.
However, there is one aspect of a commission port that
bothers me, and that is principally the reason I am speaking

June 23, 1982
Canada Ports Corporation Act
today. One of the reasons the profit picture is as good as it is, is that commission ports do not pay taxes or grants in lieu of taxes. That bothers me. I have talked to the chairman about that on numerous occasions. I have written to the minister, and the response I have received is basically bureaucratic. I know that will not change under this type of administration because that is the mentality that exists.
The one reason the administrators within the harbours section of the Ministry of Transport give for not having a commission port pay grants in lieu of taxes or taxes is that there is such a great socio-economic benefit to the community because the port is there. I admit there is. There are jobs for many stevedores. There are warehousing jobs. There are many transport jobs. There is a great socio-economic benefit to the municipality and the municipalities surrounding that commission port. Nobody denies that. Considering the amount of cash flow this commission port is generating, there has to be a lot of residual benefit to the life of that community. However, if that is true for the commission port, is it not true for Bapco Paints which is just a few miles away? Is it not true for Capital Plastics which is just a few miles away? Is it not true for the Hawker Siddeley plant which is just a few miles away? If it is true that a commission port generates socio-economic benefits to the community, surely the owner or manager of every other industry in the area would argue the same thing. Does the manager of the Bapco plant not think that the fact that he is providing jobs and payrolls to the people at his plant is of general benefit to the entire municipality? It is a specious argument on the part of the bureaucrats within the Ministry of Transport. They should not be allowed to get away with it. I object strongly to that.
Furthermore, it bothers me that when a port can make as much as $5 million in net income in one year, that that gives it an unfair competitive advantage over all other modes of transportation in the area. I think it is a truism that marine transport is the cheapest way to transport goods. It is a lot cheaper than rail or truck transport, so they have a competitive edge already. The very fact that the local truck transport depot or the railway has to pay either taxes or grants in lieu of taxes over and above the normal costs of operation puts the commission port at a distinct competitive advantage, and I do not think that is fair. Why should the commission port get a Si-million tax break, or whatever it is, when all other transport facilities have to pay the whole bill? The fact that the marine facility is not paying taxes or grants in lieu of taxes means that the tax burden for all other residents of the community has been increased. I do not think that is right or fair, and furthermore I do not think the bureaucrats within the department understand that particular problem. I do not mind if there is a port which exists only because of the socio-economic benefits it provides to its area. I do not mind if they do not pay taxes or grants in lieu of taxes as long as the federal government will make it up to that particular community. By all that is fair and right I ask the Minister of Transort (Mr. Pepin) to take note of this representation, even though all the others I have made have been ignored, and correct this injustice which is being perpetrated on the residents of Surrey municipality as a result of the installation known as the Fraser River Harbour Commission.

Mr. Speaker, I too appreciate the opportunity to speak on Bill C-92 which would envisage replacing the NHB, established by act of Parliament in 1936, with a super Crown corporation headquartered in Ottawa. In turn, it would be responsible for a number of subsidiary Crown corporations established as the need occurs to manage the financial and business affairs of various ports across Canada. I have to address this matter in light of my experience as a western Canadian, but also as a member representing a riding with rivers on two sides and the ocean on another. Therefore, in my riding there are two harbour commissions with jurisdiction over the north and south arms of the Fraser River, as well as the National Harbours Board being responsible for the major coal port facility of Roberts Bank, just off Tsawwassen. So I have some perception and views on the way in which the commissions have managed their affairs on the north and south arms of the Fraser River, as well as the board's management of the Roberts Bank super port.
Before I get into that, Mr. Speaker, I would just like to deal with the somewhat larger question of the development of west coast ports in general, especially the new coal and grain facilities at Prince Rupert, British Columbia, which come under the jurisdiction of the NHB and which represent a considerable amount of activity and a major investment by the grain consortium and federal and provincial governments. As an example of some of my concerns over Bill C-92 I would like to illustrate some of the problems we have already encountered with the development of Ridley Island. I would suggest that the passage of this bill would not in any way alleviate those problems and it would not have prevented them from occurring. I was in Prince Rupert on Saturday and talked to a number of individuals there. I had a tour of the facilities under development on Ridley Island. For example, I was made aware of a problem with a water line. The new coal port is going ahead great guns; they have cleared the site and are putting in pilings in preparation for the arrival of coal handling equipment from Japan. They have in fact been designing for a year or two a major water supply for the coal terminal. They are doing that, Mr. Speaker, in the usual federal manner, according to goldplated standards devised by government consultants and scrutineered by port officials in Prince Rupert. But ultimately this is subject to a final decision here in Ottawa. All of this goes on, of course, without reference to Parliament or the standing committee, except by hindsight.
We have discovered, Mr. Speaker, that the water line, to be
provided at a cost well in excess of $1 million, is to be supplied

In fact, that community provided a ten-inch water line in the last two or three months to Ridley Island to supply the new grain terminal, at a cost of around $300,000. This at a time when we still do not have the other line under construction. It is going to cost more than $1 million. Its capacity will be roughly the same, and the water is to be drawn from a pulp mill that really did not want to give up the water in any event. There is a total lack of appreciation for local realities when we have consultants from Vancouver and officials and administrators in Ottawa who make these final decisions. We then wonder why the cost of the terminal development rises astronomically from an original estimate of $20 million or $30 million to something approaching now $120 million to $150 million in order to develop the Ridley terminal complex. It is because of this kind of stupidity and the lack of local representation from members of local councils, trade unions, the provincial government, and especially experts in the industry there who should have known and anticipated that this problem would develop. We build these things to gold-plated standards, designed by people in Ottawa and their highly paid consultants who are generally good supporters of the Liberal Party, without any regard for the important economy that might be achieved if we used a little common sense and asked the opinion of the people at the ground level. This applies both at Prince Rupert and Vancouver with regard to the development of the waterfront and with respect to the expansion of the Roberts Bank superport.
If we recall what happened a couple of years ago, we would understand how the development of Roberts Bank proceeded. The manager of the port decided he wanted to expand Roberts Bank to five times its original acreage, without considering the other available port capacity along the north shore of Burrard Inlet; a subject upon which my colleague, the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook) and my colleague, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) had some very strong opinions. The port expansion at Roberts Bank was envisaged and created by bureaucrats, approved by experts here in Ottawa without a full appreciation of the impact it would have on the competitive port situation with regard to other existing port facilities which in some cases might well have been expanded.

Getting back to Ridley Island for a moment, we have to ask ourselves also who in their right mind and what kind of logic leads to a situation where of the some $40 million, which has been allocated to the development of the coal port, $30 million of which has already been spent offshore, and that is money allocated in the present year's estimates to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). This $30 million has been spent offshore in Japan by awarding a bid to a Japanese company which is somehow tied in to Mitsubishi, one of the companies that are purchasing the coal, and to another related Japanese company which is one of the minority shareholders in the coal fields in northeastern British Columbia, for steel piling pipe.
In both cases, we have had extreme difficulty obtaining disclosure from the minister as to the basis on which those bids were let; as to the extent to which competitive Canadian bidders were given fair consideration in the light of the different tax structures in Canada and in Japan; in light of the different tariff situations and the availibility of low interest money in Japan compared to much higher interest capital available to Canadian suppliers such as Stephens-Adamson.
What I am getting at is that under the present structure the NHB is not very accountable to this House in terms of ensuring, in its purchasing policies and in its engineering decisions, that it is getting the best value for money. That is in spite of the fact the National Harbours Board is presently accountable to Parliament through the Minister of Transport. That leads me to ask what will happen when we take that accountability away from the minister. We have heard all kinds of comments in this House in recent times that Crown corporations are there to serve in the national interest, but as they are in competition with private enterprise, they are to operate at arm's length from the minister's control. By allowing that arm's length provision these Crown corporations can often get away with blue murder. We have seen it happen. We are told these Crown corporations operate in the public interest by taking advantage of profits in good times and using them to tide the corporations through the tough times, or taking the profits from one region and using them to help out another region. I would say that all of this has built some abnormal distortions into the system in terms of suppressing the incentive of locally interested Crown corporations to improve their profit picture. Another problem has been that profits have never materialized. In the good years, Crown corporations such as Air Canada, CNR and others, have decided to reflect their profits in what they pay to their employees and what they do in terms of reinvestment and expansion of their systems. The same is true of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. I cannot mention the CBC because it never makes any profits. But these Crown corporations have never had a history of establishing a cushion or a reserve fund to tide them through the difficult periods. Now we learn, as we did a month or so ago, when the president of Air Canada came before the Standing Committee on Transport, that Air Canada-which reported bright, rosy profits last year-is in severe economic trouble. There is a suggestion that Air Canada may well be coming back to the House to get a recharge of its batteries.

Crown corporations have never proved their efficiency in terms of delivering value for money to the people of Canada.
I see the minister who was responsible for Canada Post is in the House. He knows full well that the creation of the Canada Post Corporation under the presidency of Michael Warren was just another dodge to get the government off the hook because it did not have the political courage to raise the price of a postage stamp. The government put Canada Post under the jurisdiction of a Crown corporation with the premise- provided monopoly powers were guaranteed, a question upon which we had a considerable debate a year or so ago-that suddenly a whole new streamlined and efficient postal corporation would be created. Whoever decided to increase the price of a postage stamp to 30 cents did not predict the impact that would have on the usage of the system. We might well find that in spite of the increase in revenue for a piece of mail, that Canada Post Corporation cannot possibly eliminate the deficit that Mr. Warren set out to eliminate.
Crown corporations, while they do serve certain national objectives and they have their positive features, have far too often been used by slippery politicians to get rid of a problem they have not had the courage to solve here in the House of Commons.
It is high time that we looked carefully at our record of creating new Crown corporations. We now have close to 500 Crown corporations in this country. I estimate that this bill creating a super parent corporation and all its subsidiary corporations will lead to another dozen or so Crown corporations that will be added to that list. All of these are without regard to certain criteria which would govern and limit the powers and responsibilities of Crown corporations.
1 was really interested last night when I listened to the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) speak about her party's position in relation to Bill C-92. She suggested that we should get on with this bill, get it to committee, and that it was better than what we had at present. Then she began to reel off
all the things she did not like about it, to the extent that one could not decipher from her speech what was positive or constructive about the bill or what improvements in fact would be made.
I for one believe-I do not know what will happen in committee when amendments are brought forward-that the Crown corporation to be created will lead to a situation which is worse than the present one. I should like to give some of the reasons for saying that. We on this side of the House have been arguing for a Crown corporations bill that would set out the terms of reference and the specific conditions under which Crown corporations would be established in future and would apply to existing Crown corporations. One criterion was to ensure that there was accountability to Parliament. This proposed port structure set out in Bill C-92 does not provide for accountability to Parliament any more than any other Crown corporation. The present National Harbours Board is accountable, through the Minister of Transport, as are the harbour commissions. We have to pass their estimates. We can scrutinize their financial records. We have seen how difficult it is to get information on Crown corporations through ministers. Sure, they say that they come annually with a report to the standing committee, but we remember Mr. Ediger, the president of Uranium Canada, who was called before the committee last December to explain why Eldorado Nuclear had decided to shut down Uranium City. I overheard he and the minister at the head table deciding that they should not answer any questions. I heard the minister turn to Mr. Ediger and say, "You do not have to answer those questions". Obviously not, because Crown corporations are at arm's length and they are not accountable to the House. This makes a travesty of the situation in terms of the countless abuses we see.
In the case of Uranium Canada which is being argued before the courts, we have heard the Crown attorneys argue that Crown corporations should be immune from prosecution, that they are above the law. As I understand the decision which was taken, indeed that is the case. They do not have to abide by the same laws and regulations as private sector corporations. Why do we want to create a whole series of new Crown corporations now and make them responsible for the management of our ports? They are not accountable to the law. They are not accountable to Parliament. There are no sunset provisions to ensure that when those Crown corporations have outlived their usefulness, they will be eliminated. There is no initiative taken by government to bring in a Crown corporations bill to ensure that that is the case. There is no clear-cut management structure. There is no requirement that people who are appointed to the boards of Crown corporations by order in council should be properly accredited professional people. No, in fact not. These boards are generally comprised of defeated Liberal candidates and other good friends of the Liberal Party.

In the beginning we were told that the initial government interest would be reduced to 10 per cent over a period of time, that the corporation would be used to help companies become profitable and then the government would get out. We all know that once the companies become profitable the government decides to stay in because it has described that that is the only way to help offset the deficits of further Crown corporations which are not particularly efficient in most cases.
What about local autonomy? Should a Crown Corporations bill not decide in which cases Crown corporations should have not merely titular or advisory representation at the local level but at what point they should have decisive authority at the local level? I believe that should be the case with harbour commissions and the harbour board management structure. As the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) pointed out, there is no reason for having this super corporation umbrella structure administered from Ottawa. If these corporations are supposed to operate at arm's length from the minister and from Parliament, then why has the government not had the courage to establish a bunch of regional Crown corporations to manage the ports with a high degree of local autonomy? I would like to hear the minister's answer to that. Of course, he prefers to maintain control, particularly control over budgets and over information which may or may not be passed on to Parliament. There is also the other aspect that Crown corporations have been widely used by the Liberal Party to reward its friends.
I should like to return to the Ridley Island terminal for a moment to illustrate some of my concerns as to why we need a Crown corporations bill. We have a bad enough situation in the way the Ridley terminal corporation was established. The federal government kicked in 90 per cent of the money. Ten per cent was kicked in by Federal Commerce and Navigation which was owned and operated out of Montreal by a fellow named Laddi Pathy, as well as the principals of the company. It is tied in with Paul Martin steamship interests and the like. When it came time to select an operator for the Ridley Island terminal, where one might have considered the people who live in western Canada and understand the importance of Pacific rim trade and the nature of the unique port problems out there, the federal government did not even go out to tender.
We did.

It did not even seek proposals from alternative proponents who might well have wanted to manage the port.

They are selected and appointed on the recommendation of the Minister of Transport, so that they become an instrument of political influence and little else.
I think all these aspects have to be reflected in a Crown corporations bill which sets out management structure and clear-cut limits to ministerial discretion and to the wide open windows and doors that give the minister untold latitude in the area of ministerial discretion.
What is the government afraid of? Why does it not write these limits into the present bill, unless it appreciates and approves the present situation which lends itself principally to political patronage? Will these corporations pay taxes? Will grants in lieu of taxes, about which the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta talked, for the use of municipal services on property which private businesses have to pay taxes on, be based upon the same formula by which other private businesses have to pay taxes to local authorities?
These are the kinds of things which should be set out in a Crown corporations bill before Parliament approves one more Crown corporation which will not enhance accountability to Parliament, which will not enhance financial management or the professionalism of the conduct of business affairs. In fact, it will reduce it.
For those reasons I find it very difficult to understand the position of the New Democratic party. Maybe it is not too difficult, maybe it is natural, because they are very anxious to get this bill through. The reason is that they and their friends in the Liberal Party love Crown corporations. Liberal members and members of the NDP in particular desire Crown corporations which centralize power, redistribute income and destroy the spirit of the private sector competitors. The NDP especially believes in political control and abhors individual success. Therefore, I suggest that the hon. member for Vancouver East and her colleagues on the left-hand side of the House stop pretending. They cannot have it both ways. She is not for local autonomy and her colleagues have never supported that. They want centralized authority and they want to see private companies being forced out of business so that the federal government can become increasingly involved in business.
Before we give open arms support for this piece of legislation we must carefully examine the structure of Crown corporations and the purpose for which they are being established. We have heard that the city of Vancouver would like to see speedy passage of this legislation. Mayor Mike Harcourt, who is a well-known member of the NDP, has said that he would like to see it pass quickly. Members of the NDP want to proceed quickly with this bill but we have not yet been told of one way in which this piece of legislation will improve upon the present situation. Three main virtues of this legislation have been cited. It may change. I will give it to you in committee.

Why should we in British Columbia trust the members of the government? They may say that they will bring the ceiling up to a practical limit which reflects the realities of west coast ports. Any funds transferred from a local corporation to the parent corporation would be treated as if they were deposited in a bank, to earn interest and to be subject to withdrawal by the local port depositor when they are required.
That statement sounds very positive and someone like the mayor of Vancouver, or groups like the Vancouver board of trade or the shipping interests, might have read that paper and been convinced that the government would look after them because this banking provision would allow the port of Vancouver to utilize some of its surplus earnings to plan for port expansion and major capital investments without intervention by Ottawa in an attempt to seize a major portion or all of that surplus to cross-subsidize a port somewhere else.
Without sounding selfish, western Canadians must look after some of the interests in western Canada which have been neglected by central Canada Liberal rule. We western Canadians have always shared. We need a degree of local autonomy. The government has told us that this banking system will be implemented. The mayor of Vancouver believes it and the NDP has probably fallen for it as well as some people active in the shipping industry in British Columbia. However, if it is so, why does

He stated his serious concern over the nature of the way in which the Crown corporations in this country are operated. Today we have a bill before us under which those Crown corporations will be created in much the same mould as the previous ones. I do not believe the basic problem is with Crown
corporations as such, because we do live in a mixed economic environment. I would like to point out that if we review Canadian history, we find that one of the organizations which sired the Crown corporations was the Conservative Party. We have before us the CBC and a number of others.

These Crown corporations were not created because they wanted to set some evil loose on Canada. They were simply created because it made good sense. Unfortunately, we have lost control over many of them. They are not accountable to the public, which owns them through Parliament or through the government. Unfortunately, I think that people who sit down and read the speeches of the hon. member and others in the Conservative Party will be confused because the Conservative Party is essentially confused. It fails to recognize that it is not so much that Crown corporations are opposed but, rather, their lack of accountability is objected to. I would like to point out that the province of Saskatchewan and a number of other provinces have mechanisms in place to force more accountability by Crown corporations to the people who own them.
When the bill goes to committee, I would urge the minister to consider amendments such as those which work very well with certain other Crown corporations, such as Air Canada and CN. The annual report for the new harbours organizations will come to Parliament but will unfortunately end there, in the hands of the government, with no detailed accountability provisions. If the minister were prepared to extend that one step further, he would certainly improve accountability by allowing that report to be sent to the Transport committee for study.
